reference.source: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
clinicalPearls: A salivary malignancy defined by an ETV6-NTRK3 gene fusion, morphologically analogous to secretory carcinoma of the breast.
It most often arises in the parotid but also occurs in the intraoral minor glands, typically as a slow-growing painless mass.
Many cases were historically misclassified as acinic cell carcinoma before the fusion was recognised.
Histology shows microcystic and tubular structures with abundant eosinophilic intraluminal secretions and vacuolated cytoplasm, but no true zymogen granules.
The immunophenotype is characteristic: S100, mammaglobin and SOX10 positive, with DOG1 negative, which helps separate it from acinic cell carcinoma.
The defining ETV6-NTRK3 fusion, or variant fusions such as ETV6-RET, can be demonstrated by fusion-directed molecular testing.
The NTRK fusion is therapeutically important, as it renders advanced disease potentially responsive to tropomyosin receptor kinase inhibitors.
Most tumours are indolent, but high-grade transformation is described and carries a worse outlook.
reference.pathophysiology: Secretory carcinoma is driven by a balanced translocation that fuses the ETV6 gene with NTRK3, generating a chimeric protein with constitutively active tropomyosin receptor kinase signalling that promotes proliferation and survival through downstream RAS-MAPK and PI3K pathways. The neoplastic cells display apocrine-type secretory differentiation, producing abundant intraluminal and intracytoplasmic eosinophilic secretory material within microcystic, tubular and solid architecture, closely mirroring secretory carcinoma of the breast. Unlike acinic cell carcinoma, the cells do not form true serous zymogen granules, which is reflected in a DOG1-negative, S100- and mammaglobin-positive immunophenotype. The presence of an actionable kinase fusion links the tumour's biology directly to targeted therapy, and progression is usually slow unless high-grade transformation supervenes.
additionalInvestigations: Core or excisional biopsy for histology
Immunohistochemistry including S100, mammaglobin, SOX10 and DOG1
Molecular testing for ETV6-NTRK3 and variant fusions
MRI of the primary with ultrasound or CT of the neck for staging
NTRK fusion testing to determine eligibility for targeted therapy in advanced disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable for conventional low-grade tumours treated with complete excision. Identification of the NTRK fusion offers a targeted therapy option for recurrent or metastatic disease, whereas high-grade transformation worsens the outlook.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as acinic cell carcinoma and thereby overlooking a targetable NTRK fusion
Failing to perform NTRK or fusion testing in advanced or recurrent cases
Misinterpreting DOG1 or S100 staining and reaching the wrong diagnosis
Underrecognising high-grade transformation on limited sampling
